See ''Loiseleuria.''—'''Trailing plant,''' a plant unable to support itself, but neither on the one hand ascending by the aid of tendrils or by twining, nor on the other hand creeping and rooting or lying flat, but simply growing over such objects as may present themselves. The trailing habit may, however, be combined with the climbing or the creeping.}}

'''trail'''<sup>2</sup>† (trāl), ''n.'' [< ME. ''traile,'' < OF. (and F.) ''treille,'' a trellis, a latticed frame, < L. ''trichila,'' also in inscriptions ''tricla, triclea, triclia,'' an arbor, bower. Hence ult. ''trellis.''] 1. A latticed frame; a trellis for running or climbing plants.

{{smaller block|Owt of the preas I me with-drewhe ther-fore,
And sett me doun by-hynde a ''traile''
Fulle of levis.
{{right|''Political Poems,'' etc. (ed. Furnivall), p. 58.}}}}

2. A running ornament or enrichment of leaves, flowers, tendrils, etc., as in the hollow moldings of Gothic architecture; a wreath.

{{smaller block|And over all of purest gold was spred
A ''trayle'' of yvie in his native hew.
{{right|''Spenser,'' F. Q., II. xii. 61.}}}}

{{smaller block|I bequeth to William Paston, my sone, my standing cuppe chased parcell gilt with a cover with myn armes in the botom and a flatte pece with a ''trail'' upon the cover.
{{right|''Paston Letters,'' III. 186.}}}}

'''trail'''<sup>2</sup>† (trāl), ''v. t.'' [< ''trail''<sup>2</sup>, ''n.''] To overspread with a tracery or intertwining pattern or ornament.

{{smaller block|A Camis light of purple silk, . . .
''Trayled'' with ribbands diversly distraught,
Like as the workeman had their courses taught.
{{right|''Spenser,'' F. Q., V. v. 2.}}}}

'''trail<sup>3</sup>†''' (trāl), ''n.'' [Abbr. of ''entrail'', as orig. accented on the final syllable: see ''entrail''<sup>1</sup>.] Entrails; the intestines of game when cooked and sent to table, as those of snipe and woodcock, and certain fish; also, the intestines of sheep.

{{smaller block|The thrush is presented with the ''trail,'' because the bird feeds on olives.
{{right|''Smollett'', Travels, xviii.}}}}

'''T-rail''' (tē′rāl), ''n.'' A rail with a cross-section having approximately the form of a letter T. See ''rail''<sup>1</sup>, 5.

'''trailbaston†''', ''n.'' [ME., also ''traylbaston'', ''trailebaston'', < OF. (AF.) ''trailebaston'', ''traylebaston'', prob. so called from the staves or clubs they carried, < ''trailler'', trail, + ''baston'', staff, club: see ''trail''<sup>1</sup>, ''v.'', and ''baston'', ''baton''. Roquefort gives the OF. as ''tray-le-baston'', as if < ''traire'', draw, < L. ''trahere'' (or ''traer'', < L. ''tradere'', give up) + ''le'', the, + ''baston'', staff. This view is not tenable.] In ''Eng. hist.'', one of a class of disorderly persons, banded robbers, murderers, and incendiaries, who gave great trouble in the reign of Edward I., and were so numerous that judges were appointed expressly for the purpose of trying them. See the phrases below.

For three shillings or four, or for the worth,
To beat a freeman who never did injury
To Christian body, by any evidence.

Hence ''train''1, ''n.'' For the sense 'educate,' from the lit. sense 'draw,' cf. ''educate'', ult. < L. ''educare'', draw out.] '''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To draw or drag along; trail. {{smaller block|So he hath hir ''trayned'' and drawen that the lady myght no lenger crye ne brayen. ''Merlin'' (E. E. T. S.), ii. 299.}} {{smaller block|Not distant far with heavy pace the foe
Approaching gross and huge; in hollow cube
''Training'' his devilish enginery. {{right|''Milton'', P. L., vi. 553.}}}} {{smaller block|What pitie is it that any . . . man shulde . . . be ''trayned'' . . . in to this lothesome dungeon [idleness]. {{right|''Sir T. Jonson'', Sejanus, Arg.}}}} {{smaller block|Martius Galeotti, who, by his impostures and specious falsehoods, has ''trained'' me hither into the power of my mortal enemy. {{right|''Scott'', Quentin Durward, xxviii.}}}} '''3.''' To bring into some desired course or state by means of some process of instruction and exercise. {{smaller|(''a'') To educate; instruct; rear; bring up: often with ''up''.}} {{smaller block|So was she ''trayned up'' from time to time In all chaste vertue and true bounti-hed. {{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., III. vi. 3.}}}} {{smaller block|''Train up'' a child in the way he should go, and when [even when, R. V.] he is old he will not depart from it. {{right|Prov. xxii. 6.}}}} {{smaller block|You have ''trained'' me like a peasant. {{right|''Shak.'', As you Like it, i. 1. 71.}}}} {{smaller|(''b'') To make proficient or efficient, as in some art or profession, by instruction, exercise, or discipline; make proficient by instruction or drill: as, to ''train'' nurses; to ''train'' soldiers.}} {{smaller block|And when Abram heard that his brother was taken captive, he armed his ''trained'' servants. {{right|Gen. xiv. 14.}}}} {{smaller block|''Trained'' in camps, he knew the art To win the soldier's hardy heart. {{right|''Scott'', Marmion, iii. 4.}}}} {{smaller|(''c'') To tame or render docile; exercise in the performance of certain tasks or tricks: as, to ''train'' dogs or monkeys.}} {{smaller block|Animals can be ''trained'' by man, but they cannot ''train'' themselves. They can be taught some accomplishments, formed to some new habits; but where man has not done this for them they remain uneducated. {{right|''J. F. Clarke'', Self-Culture, p. 33.}}}} {{smaller block|(''d'') To fit by proper exercise and regimen for the performance of some feat; render capable of enduring the strain incident to a contest of any kind, by a course of suitable exercise, regimen, etc.; put in suitable condition, as for a race, by preparatory exercise, etc.: as, to ''train'' a boat's crew for a race. (''e'') To give proper or some particular shape or direction to by systematic manipulation or extension; specifically, in ''gardening'', to extend the branches of, as on a wall, espalier, etc.}} {{smaller block|Tell her, when I'm gone, to ''train'' the rose-bush that I set About the parlour-window. {{right|''Tennyson'', May Queen, New-Year's Eve.}} Why will she ''train'' that winter curl In such a spring-like way? {{right|''O. W. Holmes'', My Aunt.}}}} '''4.''' To bring to bear; direct or aim carefully: as, to ''train'' a gun upon a vessel or a fort. {{smaller block|Again and again we set up the camera, and ''trained'' it upon a part of the picturesque throng. {{right|''G. Kennan'', The Century, XXXVIII. 73.}}}} {{smaller block|'''To train a scent'''†, in ''hunting'', same as ''to carry a scent.'' See phrase under ''scent.''}} {{smaller block|I ha' seene one Sheepe worry a dozen Foxes, By Moon-shine, in a morning before day, They hunt, ''trayne-sents'' with Oxen, and plow with Dogges. {{right|''Brome'', The Antipodes, i. 6.}}}} {{smaller block|'''To train fine.''' See ''fine''2. ='''Syn. 3.''' To school, habituate, inure. See ''instruction.''}} '''II.''' ''intrans.'' '''1'''†. To be attracted or lured. {{smaller block|The highest soaring Hauke ''traineth'' to ye lure. {{right|''Lyly'', Euphues, Anat. of Wit, p. 35.}}}} '''2.''' To exercise; impart proficiency by practice and use; drill; discipline. {{smaller block|Nature ''trains'' while she teaches; she disciplines the powers while she imparts information to the intellect. {{right|''J. F. Clarke'', Self-Culture, Int., p. 11.}}}} '''3.''' To fit one's self for the performance of some feat by preparatory regimen and exercise. {{smaller block|So he resolved at once to ''train'',
And walked and walked with all his main. {{right|''W. S. Gilbert'', Perils of Invisibility.}}}} '''4.''' To be under training, as a recruit for the army; be drilled for military service.—'''5.''' To travel by train or by rail: sometimes with an indefinite ''it.'' [Colloq.] {{smaller block|From Aberdeen to Edinburgh we ''trained it'' by easy stages. {{right|''Harper's Mag.'', LXXVII. 954.}}}} '''6.''' ''train'', a train, retinue, herd (of cattle), pace, course, way, bustle, train of boats or cars, etc., = Pr. ''trahi'' = Sp. ''trajin'', ''trajino'', formerly ''train'', ''trayno'', = It.
